fullPassage: In Earth’s tectonic history, one of the most intriguing spots on the planet is Ireland, for despite its relatively small area, the movement of its land would give it the distinction of an unusually diverse geology. Hundreds of millions of years ago, Ireland’s northern region existed on the continent of Laurentia, which forms parts of North America today, and the southern part was located on the continent of Gondwana, which now composes sections of Europe, Africa, and Australia. The two continents were initially divided by an ocean, but later, as the ocean closed, they collided and combined. The force of this collision created immense pressure, resulting in significant geological changes. It caused the formation of mountain ranges with a northeast-to-southwest orientation —the same direction as the boundary along which the continents converged. It also triggered the transformation of existing rock, creating some new types. Then the land steadily drifted north and was covered by water, which further diversified its geology by allowing for the formation of sedimentary deposits on the island.
